value.body: Finds, checks and reports news and stories for newspapers, TV, radio, websites and digital platforms. Journalists work as reporters on a beat (city, politics, business, courts, sports), as sub-editors and desk staff, or as freelancers. A day may involve calls and field reporting, verifying facts, writing to deadline and working with editors.

items.label: Typical entry
items.note: A diploma or degree in journalism or mass communication is common

items.label: Common tools
items.value: Content management systems, basic audio/video editing, fact-checking methods

items.label: Languages
items.value: English and Indian-language media both hire

items.label: Periodicals in PRGI database
items.note: Registered newspapers and periodicals; many registered titles are inactive
items.source: Press Registrar General of India (as reported)

value.title: How you get in
value.body: Freshers usually enter through internships at newspapers, channels or digital outlets, or after a journalism diploma — for example from the Indian Institute of Mass Communication, which admits by entrance test. A portfolio of published work, including campus or freelance pieces, counts for a lot. Strong writing in an Indian language opens the large regional-language media sector.

value.title: Skills you'll use
items: Basic photo, audio or video editing

value.title: At a glance
items: Starting roles are often trainee reporter or sub-editor, with long and irregular hours.
Growth path: reporter → senior correspondent → editor, or moves into data, video or investigative journalism.
Media hiring is uneven; many journalists also freelance or move into communications work.
